title: Control Plane DNS split-horizon + TTL propagation postmortem and runbook draft
content:
Summary:

Between 2025-12-18 03:12 UTC and 2025-12-18 07:04 UTC several Private/VPC customers experienced intermittent control-plane reachability failures: API calls to the control plane returned TLS handshake errors or timed out, SDKs retried repeatedly, and some long-running streams aborted. The failures correlated with a DNS change deployed during a routine edge/CA rotation that unintentionally created a split-horizon discrepancy between public DNS and a set of customer private hosted zones. High TTLs (3600s) caused slow propagation and many customers kept resolving to stale IPs for several hours.

Impact:
- Affected surface: Redwood Private control plane endpoints for ~12 customer VPCs across two regions (us-west-2, eu-west-1).
- Symptom: TLS handshake errors (SNI mismatch), intermittent SYN retries, increased latency, and failed streaming responses.
- Severity: P2 for some enterprise customers (lost control plane connectivity during batch jobs, failed rollouts).~(See JIRA-INC-2983 for customer list).
- Duration: ~3h 52m from first alerts to mitigation fully propagated; residual client-side cache issues extended visible impact up to ~8 hours for some customers.

Timeline (high level):
- 2025-12-18 03:12 UTC: Synthetic monitors from the Private control-plane health check alert (PagerDuty -> PD oncall).
- 03:18 UTC: Multiple customer SREs pinged #sre-private-deployments reporting TLS handshake errors and elevated retries.
- 03:25 UTC: Oncall team begins triangulation: TLS code path failing early; client attempts show server IPs that don't match expected control-plane pool.
- 03:40 UTC: Ops engineer notices an automated DNS update rolled out at 03:05 UTC (edge certificate rotation) which replaced an A record in the public zone; further investigation shows a related Terraform apply attempted to update private hosted zones but failed on cross-account permissions.
- 04:05 UTC: Temporary mitigation: rollback of the public A record change to previous IP set initiated to stop new resolvers from receiving the new mapping.
- 04:40 UTC: Workaround: we pushed an emergency run (manual apply) to customer private hosted zones where we had access (5/12) to reconcile records; communicated with customers for those we couldn't access.
- 06:00 UTC: Reduced TTLs and additional cache-flush guidance sent to customers; we validated propagation for most customer zones.
- 07:04 UTC: PagerDuty alerts quiet; monitoring shows healthy connectivity.

Root cause analysis (why this happened):
1) Change window + insufficient pre-change sequencing: During an edge certificate rotation we updated a public-facing A record as part of the rollout. That change was meant to be mirrored to customer private hosted zones (split-horizon) via an automated Terraform pipeline. The public change happened before successful propagation to all private hosted zones.
2) Automation failure + insufficient guardrails: The Terraform apply that updates private zones failed due to a recently-introduced IAM policy tightening in the infra account. The failure did not block the public update; the pipeline continued (no pre-checks to enforce parity). The pipeline lacked a built-in precondition that would abort the public commit if the private-hosted-zone step failed.
3) High TTLs and client caching: Both our public zone and many customer private hosted zones were configured with TTL=3600s. When some resolvers saw the new public record, they cached it for an hour; customer's resolvers inside VPCs continued to serve the old IPs. The mismatch between resolver caches caused traffic to split between old and new backends, and the new backend did not have the matching TLS configuration for the customer SNI, producing handshake failures.
4) Lack of DNS discrepancy monitoring: We have synthetic control-plane checks, but no automated comparator that queries both public and known customer private hosted zones to detect mismatches early.

Contributing factors:
- Recent IAM policy changes weren't communicated to the runbook owners; the automation had no self-test or alert on failure.
- Documentation gap: runbook did not specify lowering TTLs before rolling DNS changes for split-horizon endpoints.
- Partial access: for several customers we do not have cross-account route53 access; manual reconciliation required and that took longer.

Immediate mitigations performed:
- Rolled back public DNS A record to prior value (stop the migration in-flight).
- Manual apply of corrected records to 5/12 private hosted zones where we had access.
- Coordinated with affected customers to perform cache flushes, VPN reconnections, or restart of local DNS resolvers where needed.
- Shortened TTLs to 60s for future changes on the public zone and advised customers to set lower TTLs during planned switchover windows.

Longer-term remediation and action items (owner - ETA):
1) Add precondition gates to the DNS deployment pipeline: fail-public-change-if-private-apply-fails (owner: Ravi N. - ETA: 2026-01-31).
2) Create a DNS parity monitor that queries public zone vs customer private hosted zone mappings and raises an automated alert if mismatches are detected (owner: Lena O. - ETA: 2026-02-28).
3) Update runbook to require lowering TTL to <= 60s at least 1 hour before any split-horizon change; create automation to set/restore TTLs in both public and private zones (owner: Jonas P. - ETA: 2026-01-15).
4) Improve IAM change communication: add infra-team checklist item to announce IAM policy changes that affect automation 72 hours before enforcement (owner: Aisha G. - ETA: 2026-01-08).
5) For customers where we lack hosted-zone access, add a pre-notification template and a self-service Terraform module customers can apply to enable safe, automated reconciliation (owner: Product Solutions - ETA: 2026-03-15).
6) Post-deployment smoke test: extend synthetic checks to verify TLS SNI for each customer mapping from multiple vantage points including inside-customer-VPC simulators where feasible (owner: eng-sre - ETA: 2026-02-14).
7) Add logging/telemetry to DNS automation pipeline: emit a clear success/failure event with target zone list and error context to the incident bus (owner: infra-release - ETA: 2026-01-22).

Draft runbook for future split-horizon DNS changes (delta from current):
- Pre-change (T-72h): Communicate planned change to infra-runbook list and affected customers; declare maintenance window; check IAM policies.
- Pre-change (T-1h): Lower TTL to 60s for public and private zones (or advise customers to do so); ensure the DNS pipeline dry-run finishes with parity.
- Change (T0): Perform change in public zone, then private zone; verify automation returns success. If private apply fails, abort further propagation and initiate rollback of public changes.
- Immediate verification (T+5m): Run DNS parity monitor and synthetic TLS SNI checks from 3 vantage points (public, us-west-2 VPC, eu-west-1 VPC).
- Post-change (T+1h): Restore TTLs to normal values; record change in change log.
- Rollback criteria: sustained >0.5% error rate for >5 minutes on control-plane synthetic checks, or any authenticated customer reports of TLS handshake failures.

Notes / open questions:
- Do we want an automated ability to update private hosted zones for customers via cross-account stack sets? Security and customer consent considerations need product input.
- Evaluate whether moving control-plane endpoints to a stable IP set (multi-A) with proper TLS certs per SNI is a better long-term approach to reduce DNS flip risk.

Communication and customer handling:
- We created a customer advisory template and sent a targeted message to impacted customers within 90 minutes of detection outlining the cause and recommended client-side steps.
- Follow-up 24h summary: drafted tailored remediation instructions for each customer, and offered a scheduled session to help apply DNS fixes where we couldn't do it ourselves.

Appendix: quick forensics notes (raw):
- dig +trace of controlplane.redwood.private.example.com from public resolver at 03:22 UTC returned new IP set (A: 54.84.12.11).
- dig from one affected customer VPC resolver returned old IP (A: 10.2.1.45) which was still the active backend for some nodes.
- Terraform logs: infra-dns-apply job #742 showed a 403 error when attempting to write to account:customer-123-zone at 03:06 UTC (cause: IAM policy enforce).
- TLS errors in logs: "tls: handshake failure (remote error: tls: bad certificate)" correlated with SNI header being controlplane.redwood.private.example.com served by new edge with a different cert set.

If you have edits or additional diagnostics to add, paste outputs from customer dig traces and Terraform logs into the confluence linked above and tag the owners.

This doc is a working postmortem + runbook draft; next formalized version will be published after action items are assigned and initial remediation work is validated.
